On Wednesday, June 29, 2022 at 11:34:55 PM UTC+9 tucke...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Austin,
>
> The independent pathways model can be specified to operate on the first order factors (rather than the higher order factors) or on the individual traits. You should interpret accord to which specification you use. I can imagine wanting to specify on the first order factors (so it's still a common pathways model through those factors but not through the higher order factor), and then from there specifying yet another independent pathways model to operate on the individual traits (or perhaps several, where you free up independent pathways for one first order factor at a time). That way you can get at heterogeneity at each level.
>
> You can read through the 11 disorder paper by Grotzinger et al. in Nature Genetics to see the approach that we specifically took for the hierarchical p factor model.
>
> I can't recall off hand what the defaults are for allowing independent variables to correlate with factors. When you run the model in some tests SNPs with your code you should make sure that the SNP doest covary with the factor(s) by default (you can always fix those covariances to 0 to be sure) in your independent pathways model.
>
> Elliot
>
> On Wed, Jun 29, 2022 at 4:29 AM Austin Park <sh.aust...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi, I'm trying to run an independent pathway model to obtain a heterogeneity index for a hierarchical model.
> >
> > The model in which SNP operates through the factor was specified as below.
> >
> > model <- "F1 =~ 1*V8 + V7 + V6 + V3
> >         F2 =~ 1*V1 + V2 + V6 + V5 + V3
> >         F3 =~ 1*V4 + V5 + V6
> >         M =~ 1*F1 + F2 + F3
> >         V5 ~~ a*V5
> >         a > 0.001
> >         M ~ SNP
> >         "
> >
> >
> > And below is how I am planning to specify an independent pathway.
> >
> > model <- "F1 =~ 1*V8 + V7 + V6 + V3
> >         F2 =~ 1*V1 + V2 + V6 + V5 + V3
> >         F3 =~ 1*V4 + V5 + V6
> >         M =~ 1*F1 + F2 + F3
> >         V5 ~~ a*V5
> >         a > 0.001
> >         V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5 + V6 + V7 + V8 ~ SNP
> >         "
> >
> > I just want to double-check if this is the correct way to represent the independent pathway for the second-order factor (M) of the hierarchical model. Should the SNP effect be on the first-order factors or the genetic indicators?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Austin

messages.subject: Prerequisite data modification for running CommonfactorGWAS
messages.subject_clean: Prerequisite data modification for running CommonfactorGWAS
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We are using Genomic SEM's commonfactorGWAS to generate summary statistics with 7 trait components of Metabolic syndrome. Our aim is to generate a PRS score for Metabolic syndrome.
Some of the GWAS summary statistics used are presented in reference to the allele on the forward strand while others are in the reverse strand. Our questions are the following:

1- Should the summary statistics reported on the reverse strands be flipped to the forward strand before munging (i.e. ensure same direction across all files)?

2- Additionally, some of our traits are from the same cohort study. Is it okay to munge GWAS  summary statistics if some of the component traits are from the same study population/cohort?

3- Should the effect allele be arranged such that the allele shows increased risk?

Thanks you for your time!

Best regards,
Nada

messages.subject: Re: Prerequisite data modification for running CommonfactorGWAS
messages.subject_clean: Prerequisite data modification for running CommonfactorGWAS
messages.body_plain:
For standard sumstats, munge should take care of aligning to a common ref panel etc...
Please be sure to consult the wiki and our papers (especially https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0566-x1).
One particular strength of Genomic SEM is that the sumstats can come from samples with varying and/or unknown degrees of overlap. However, traits that are directly computed as linear composites of other traits from the same sample that are in your analysis should not be included (i.e. you should not be able to predict one trait from the other traits with R2=100%), as this would introduce inappropriate dependencies in the data.

messages.subject: User specified model; independent pathways model for subsequent Q calculations
messages.subject_clean: User specified model; independent pathways model for subsequent Q calculations
messages.body_plain:
To all,

My models are as follows tested with first 10 snps:

# User specified model (factor loading for PHENO1 > 1)
modelCF<-"F1 =~ PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > .001
F1 ~ SNP"
pfactorCF <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats_test, model = modelCF, sub=c("F1~SNP"))

# Alt user specified model (factor loading for PHENO1 > 1)
modelCFalt <-"F1 =~ NA*PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
F1 ~~1*F1
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > .001
F1 ~ SNP"
pfactorCFalt <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats_test, model = modelCFalt, sub=c("F1~SNP"))

# Independent pathways model - to calculate Q
modelIPM<-"F1 =~ NA*PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
F1 ~~1*F1
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > .001
PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3 ~ SNP"
pfactorIPM <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats_test, model = modelIPM)

I have 2 questions:
1. What is the difference between modelCF and modelCFalt?  I added the F1~~1*F1 and NA* for first phenotype, thinking that it was redundant to modelCF specification  (PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1 and a > .001).  The estimates and SEs are different by approximately a factor of 4.11 (but approximately) with approximately the same Z and Pval_Estimates.

2. For the Independent pathways model, as set up, generates 10 lines for each SNP (for each permutation e.g. F1=~PHENO1, F1=~PHENO2, F1=~PHENO3, PHENO1~~PHENO1, PHENO1~SNP, ..., F1~~F1), with different values for est, se, etc, but same chisq and chisq_df=0.  I figure there is something wrong with my model specification or the userGWAS code.

Thanks!

Dan

messages.subject: Re: User specified model; independent pathways model for subsequent Q calculations
messages.subject_clean: User specified model; independent pathways model for subsequent Q calculations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

Good questions!

1. The difference is how the estimates are scaled. So in modelCF unit loading identification is automatically being used where the loading of the first indicator on the factor is fixed to 1, and then all the estimates are going to shift around to reflect that loading. In modelCFalt you are specifying unit variance identification where the variance of the factor is fixed to 1 and that first loading is freely estimated. They are statistically equivalent, just different ways of scaling the estimates, which is why you get the same p-values and z-statistics.

2. If you don't specify anything for the sub argument, then userGWAS will save all components of the model for each SNP (not recommended just for memory reasons). So for each SNP it is showing the full set of model results, and then printing the same model chi-square on each line since this is the model fit for the same model (a bit confusing I know, but we figured it was better than having a completely separate list object of model fit indices that you then have to match up with each SNP).

Best,
  Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Thanks! As re: question 2, I only figured I had misspecified my model or missed something that belonged under userGWAS().  So if I included sub=c("F1~~F1")  then that would give me one line for each SNP with the chisq stat and chisq df needed to calculate the Q index per SNP?

Another question, sort of related.  I ran a replication model, but this time the common factor model without individual SNP effects (run preliminary to the model with SNP effects) did not indicate a Heywood problem - none of the loading factors > 1 and there was no negative variances.  So I ran this model using the commonfactorGWAS function.  However, some of the SNPs generated a warning of negative variances.  Actually, even running the userGWAS models above (modelCF and modelCFalt), there were some SNPs generating a negative variance warning (but not many, may .001%).

So my question 3: should I run the replication model using the userGWAS function with variances constrained, or just drop the SNPs with the warnings?

Thanks again!

Dan
